listenings.text: I have been coaching people through second languages for about fifteen years, and there is one month I can predict without knowing anything about the student. It is usually the fourth. Everything before it feels wonderful. In the first two months every single lesson gives you something you could not do the week before, and that is not because you are brilliant. It is because almost everything was missing, so almost anything you add is visible. Then the basics are in place, the gains get smaller, and the whole thing levels off. That is the month people tell me they have stopped improving, and it is the month most of them quit. What I try to explain, and I am not always successful, is that a plateau is not a signal that something has gone wrong. It is what improvement looks like once it becomes incremental. You are still getting better. You have simply lost the ability to feel it, because the changes are now smaller than the difference between a good day and a bad day. So I ask every student to keep one thing: a written record of something specific they could not do a month ago. Not a feeling, a sentence. And the students who keep that record are, almost without exception, the ones who are still here a year later.

A study that gets quoted a great deal in this area followed two groups of adult learners for six months. Same material, same schedule, same teachers, and only one difference between them. The first group turned up and studied. The second group turned up, studied, and then wrote down a single number at the end of every session. It did not much matter which number, as long as it was the same one every time. Six months later, the second group was far more likely to still be attending, and the gap did not open up at the beginning. It opened at exactly the point where progress stopped being obvious, which was somewhere around the fourth month. The researchers were fairly careful about the explanation. They did not think the second group was more motivated, because motivation was measured at the start and the two groups were the same. What they suggested is much simpler and, I think, more useful. Without a record, the only thing you can compare today with is how you remember feeling last week, and nobody remembers that accurately. With a record, you compare it with something written down. The number is not the point. Having something outside your own head to argue with is the point.

defs: happening in small steps rather than all at once
an important point in a longer process

a standard you measure your progress against

paras: There is a shape that almost every long project makes, and anybody who has tried to learn something as an adult has seen it. The first weeks are extraordinary. Every session gives you something you could not do before, and it is tempting to read that as talent. It is not. At the start almost everything is missing, so almost anything you add shows. Then the obvious gaps close, what is left is smaller and harder, and the curve levels off. Nothing has gone wrong. The improvement has simply become incremental, and incremental improvement is invisible from the inside.

This is where people stop, and they stop for a reason that sounds sensible when they say it out loud. They are not getting anywhere. They have hit a plateau, and a plateau feels like evidence. What makes it convincing is that the only comparison available is memory: you compare how today felt with how you think last month felt, and memory is not built for that job. It smooths, it flatters the recent past, and it will report no change through a period of steady change. If the choice is between a feeling and nothing, the feeling wins every time.

The way out is unglamorous and it is nearly always the same. Write something down. Not a score out of ten and not a mood — one specific thing you could not do a month ago and can do now. It becomes a benchmark, and the value of a benchmark is not that it motivates you. It is that it is outside your head, so it does not change when you are tired. People who keep one are dramatically more likely to stick with what they started, and the difference does not appear in the enthusiastic first months. It appears exactly where the curve goes flat.

It helps to be precise about a word people use loosely. Somebody who studied a language years ago and then stopped is not bad at it — they are rusty, which is a different problem with a different solution. What they lost was access, not knowledge, and what they need is not to start over but to be put back under pressure. Somebody who has fallen behind after years away usually finds that the first month is much faster than they had feared, and the fourth is much slower than they had hoped.

So the useful question is not whether you are improving. Over any short window you cannot answer that honestly, and the attempt is what makes people quit. The useful question is whether you are still going, and whether there is a record. A milestone is not the same thing as a finish line. It is a place you can stand and look back from, and the only reason it works is that somebody wrote down where they were standing before.
